extraction.name: Vibravox
extraction.description: A GDPR-compliant dataset of French speech captured with five different body-conduction audio sensors and one airborne reference microphone. It contains 45 hours per sensor of speech samples and physiological sounds recorded by 188 participants under different acoustic conditions, with annotations about recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions.
extraction.creator: Julien Hauret, Malo Olivier, Thomas Joubaud, Christophe Langrenne, Sarah Poiree, Veronique Zimpfer, Eric Bavu
extraction.citeAs: J. Hauret, M. Olivier, C. Langrenne, S. Poiree, and E. Bavu, "vibravox (revision 071945b)," 2024. https://huggingface.co/datasets/Cnam-LMSSC/vibravox
extraction.rai:dataCollection: The dataset was created through a controlled recording protocol using six simultaneously recorded sensors: five body-conduction microphones and one airborne reference microphone. A total of 200 participants were recorded in four consecutive steps: speech-clean (15 minutes of reading sentences sourced from French Wikipedia), speechless-noisy (2 minutes 24 seconds of silence in spatialized noise), speechless-clean (54 seconds of silence), and speech-noisy (54 seconds of reading in spatialized noise). Recordings were made with a Zoom F8n at 48 kHz and 32 bits in a 3D sound spatializer with 56 loudspeakers for noisy conditions. After post-processing, 188 participants were retained.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionType: Direct measurement, Experiments, Software Collection, Manual Human Curator
extraction.rai:dataCollectionMissingData: A small number of audio clips had shortcomings such as mispronounced sentences, sensors shifting from their initial positions, occasional sensor malfunctions, or a microphone inadvertently left unequipped. Post-processing excluded 6% of participants and 6.8% of pronounced sentences.
extraction.rai:dataCollectionRawData: Raw data consist of simultaneous audio recordings from a headset microphone, forehead accelerometer, soft in-ear microphone, rigid in-ear microphone, throat microphone, and temple vibration pickup. Text read by participants comes from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice. Ambient noise excerpts were sourced largely from AudioSet and from in-house ambisonic recordings of concerts and street events.
extraction.rai:dataManipulationProtocol: The text from the French Wikipedia subset of Common Voice was filtered to exclude most proper names, numbers, Greek letters, mathematical symbols, and syntactic errors. Text was normalized by lowercasing and removing punctuation except apostrophes. For speech enhancement in noisy conditions, the authors dynamically mixed speech-clean with speechless-noisy to create synthetic noisy training data, but this is described as an experimental use of the dataset rather than part of the released dataset construction.
extraction.rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: A 20 Hz high-pass filter was uniformly applied to each acquisition channel during recording. Post-processing used three automatic filters on speech-clean utterances: PER[j] < 10%, SNR[i,j] > 1.5 dB, and Lspeech50[i,j] > Lsilence50[i]. Indicators were extracted using whisper-timestamped for alignment and voice activity detection, Levenshtein distance for phoneme error rate, and percentile sound levels for speech and silence. If a sample passed all filters, VAD timestamps were extended by 0.6 seconds on both sides; if adjusted boundaries exceeded the original audio, the audio was trimmed by 15 ms on the affected side. Only filtered speech-clean samples were added, and the other three subsets were kept for a participant if the corresponding speech-clean subset was not empty. The final dataset was split by speaker into 80% train, 10% validation, and 10% test, balanced by male and female speakers.
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Annotations include recording conditions and linguistic transcriptions. The textual data were normalized and converted to phonetic transcriptions in the International Phonetic Alphabet using the CoML lab text phonemizer. For words not correctly handled by the phonemizer, a phase of manual phonetic transcription was performed for unrecognized words such as "algorithme".
extraction.rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The authors used phonetic labeled transcriptions and compared them with phonetic transcriptions derived from Whisper output using Levenshtein distance to compute phoneme error rate as part of post-processing. A filter discarded samples with PER greater than 10% to ensure high-quality labels for the speech-to-phonemes task.
extraction.rai:machineAnnotationTools: CoML lab text phonemizer, whisper-timestamped, Whisper
extraction.rai:personalSensitiveInformation: Gender and age of participants are reported. The paper also states compliance with GDPR, informed consent, anonymization, and encryption of data during storage and analysis.
extraction.rai:dataSocialImpact: The dataset is intended to drive progress in body-conducted speech analysis and support the development of robust communication systems for real-world applications, particularly in noisy environments. The paper discusses applications in military operations, industrial settings, access control, intelligence gathering, voice commands, and monitoring vital signs such as heart rate.
extraction.rai:dataBiases: The paper notes that existing datasets often lack scale and diversity, and states that a deliberate effort was made to recruit a diverse and gender-balanced group of participants to increase representativeness and inclusivity. It also reports that the dataset was split with 80% of male and female speakers in training, 10% in validation, and 10% in test. The paper discusses that some in-ear microphone performance issues may arise from ear canal anatomy not fitting a one-size-fits-all design.
extraction.rai:dataLimitations: The dataset is in French, which limits language coverage. Although 200 participants were recorded, only 188 were retained after filtering. The post-processing filters did not catch all issues, for example when a participant's ear canal was too small for the rigid in-ear microphone to achieve proper acoustic sealing. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference. The paper also notes trade-offs between noise robustness and bandwidth across sensors, and that the dataset was curated for rigorous analysis and fair comparison rather than maximizing overall performance.
extraction.rai:dataUseCases: The dataset is intended for training, validation, and testing of speech-related tasks including speech enhancement, bandwidth extension, speech-to-phonemes recognition, speaker verification, voice commands, and monitoring vital signs such as heart rate. The speech-clean subset contains most of the training data. The speech-noisy subset primarily serves testing purposes because it lacks a clean reference. The speechless-noisy subset can be combined with speech-clean recordings for data augmentation while retaining a clean reference. The speechless-clean subset can be used for tasks such as heart rate tracking, analyzing sensor noise properties, or generating synthetic datasets with realistic physiological and sensor-inherent noise.
